extracted_by: hand, T-0261 — the Chicago American read, June to August 1835
note: Volume I, Number 10, and the best-set local column since 20 June. Three things the corpus did not have: a physician's office placed ON LAKE STREET, NEAR THE POST OFFICE; a stove and hollow-ware stock, which is the first heating and cooking evidence in the run; and the school of 1835-08-01 revealed as a school FOR YOUNG LADIES, with a fee scale that disagrees with the earlier printing's. The post office's opening hour, cut in every earlier notice, is legible here: six o'clock in the morning.

claims.notes: A PHYSICIAN'S OFFICE WITH A REAL ADDRESS — 'on Lake street, near the Post Office' — and it puts a useful constraint on the post office at the same time. T-0257's Democrat fixture places J. S. C. Hogan's store 'one [door from] the Post Office' in SOUTH WATER STREET, and 1835-07-04 of this run shows Hogan is the postmaster; this card says the post office is near enough to Lake Street to be a Lake Street anchor. Both can be true where the two streets are close or at a corner between them, and the two together are worth more than either alone. THE MEDICINE IS THE OTHER HALF OF THE CLAIM: a botanic practitioner, Old School trained but practising the reformed New York and Ohio system, advertising vegetable remedies AGAINST mercury by name. Chicago in August 1835 has an allopath (Barnard, at the New York House in Lake Street), a botanic (Austin, in Lake Street), two druggists and a travelling dentist — a medical street, which is a thing a reconstruction can say about a frontage.

claims.notes: HOW A CHICAGO HOUSE WAS HEATED AND COOKED IN, in the town's own words and for the first time in this corpus: COOKING STOVES in several patterns 'with complete furniture', COAL STOVES, box stoves, and hollow ware and castings from a named ironworks. That bears directly on this project's chimneys and roof stacks — a town buying cooking stoves is not a town of open hearths only, and the stack question (T-0137) has been argued without any evidence of this kind. THE MAKERS' NAMES AND THE IRONWORKS ARE CUT and are left inside `[uncertain: …]`; so is the seller's signature, which the segmenter has taken entirely, so the business is recorded under an explicit non-name. Dart & Co. advertised castings a fortnight earlier and MAY be the same seller; no attribution is made.

claims.notes: THE SCHOOL OF 1835-08-01 IS A SCHOOL FOR YOUNG LADIES, and it does not exist yet as a permanent one: it will become permanent 'should sufficient encouragement be offered', and prospective subscribers are to leave their names before the fall term opens on Monday the 10th. So on the scene date Chicago has fee-paying schooling being organised, and no school building of any kind documented. THE FEES DISAGREE WITH THE EARLIER PRINTING and this claim does not reconcile them: 1835-08-01 reads '81100' and '88,00' where this one reads '6.00' and '87,00'. $6.00 and $7.00 for the ordinary and higher English branches are internally consistent with each other and with a Latin-and-French rate above them; the earlier printing's figures are single-pass OCR of the same advertisement and are the ones to distrust. Both quotes stand as printed.

claims.notes: SIX O'CLOCK IN THE MORNING — the post office's opening hour, cut out of both earlier printings of this notice (1835-07-04 and 07-11) and legible here. A town office open from six, kept open after hours whenever a mail comes in, and opening on Sundays too: that is the rhythm of the building, and it is the kind of detail that tells a reconstruction when its streets were busy. The same notice has now run in four consecutive issues over five weeks, each time damaged in a different place, and between them the whole of it is recovered.

claims.notes: THE FIRST WEEK OF AUGUST IN THE PORT, and two ports appear that the earlier columns never named: SACKETT'S HARBOR at the far end of Lake Ontario, and KALAMAZOO. With Milwaukee, Buffalo, St. Joseph, Green Bay, Detroit, Root River and Michigan City from the previous columns, the American's shipping list now gives this project eight named ports in regular contact with the Chicago river in the summer of 1835 — which is the trading world the town's wharves actually served, stated rather than assumed.

claims.notes: A WHOLESALE SPIRITS AND GROCERY STOCK BY THE CASK, in quantities that say what a Chicago storehouse held: thirty hogsheads of St. Croix rum, sixteen of American brandy, twelve more of rum, four pipes of pine-apple gin and twenty-five bushels of dried apples, with young Hyson tea alongside. Recorded as `price` rather than `business` because no seller survives in either span — the signatures at the foot of both lists are taken by the segmenter — so this documents the TRADE and not a firm. Consistent with the Harmon, Loomis stock lists of June and with Hubbard & Co.'s provisions in July: the town's wholesale trade is spirits, groceries and provisions in bulk, arriving by lake and going out to the country.
